title: The Condition for Rebirth
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The condition for rebirth: the ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death.

inline.s: The condition for rebirth:
the ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death
This very condition for rebirth,
is what Master Shandao, a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, and Master Yongming, also a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha,
together with the realized Masters Tanluan and Daochuo, have taught; it is
a
statement of sacred authority
Those who are mindful of the Buddha must, above all, be clear about this:
What is the condition for rebirth?
Otherwise, one races in the wrong direction,
and ruins the great matter of one's own rebirth.
The condition for rebirth,
is the
very heart
of the Pure Land school.
It determines how the teaching master gives guidance,
how the student cultivates,
so as to ensure rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss
[Statement of sacred authority] This is spoken by the sages, correct and without error, and may certainly be received with faith.

Question: I have already made up my mind that I must be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and that no matter how painful or exhausting, I will press on with unremitting vigor. But I must first be clear about what the condition for rebirth is, so that I know how to apply my effort. Please tell me plainly: what is the condition for rebirth?
Answer:
The condition for rebirth is:
the ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death.
That is to say,

as long as, at the moment of death, the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha continues through ten thoughts (without being cut off by deluded thought), one is in mutual resonance with Amitabha Buddha and, received by the Buddha, is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Ten thoughts at the moment of death; continuous, and rebirth follows.
[Continuity] The thought of mindfulness of the Buddha is joined from one moment to the next, not interrupted by deluded thought.
[Mutual resonance] The response of sentient beings and the response of Amitabha Buddha are in mutual communication.

Therefore, to ensure rebirth, in ordinary times one must not only accomplish "ten thoughts continuous, habit becoming nature," but must also cultivate blessings and accumulate virtue, so as to avoid obstacles and hindrances appearing at the moment of death.
Question: What is the basis for saying that "the condition for rebirth is the ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death"?
Answer:
As for how one can be reborn
Master Shandao taught:
"Continuity brings rebirth
at the moment of death,
as long as the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha continues (not interrupted by deluded thought), one is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)
. If one can be mindful thought after thought without break, to the end of life,
(one who thus practices through his whole life)
, then ten of ten are reborn, a hundred of a hundred."
(See
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teachings
in the section "Continuity brings rebirth".)
Master Shandao is a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha; his words are the words of Amitabha Buddha, so he, of course, is the authority on the condition for rebirth
! This is the basis.
As for how
one can be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss
, Master Shandao, a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, spoke very clearly
(See
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teachings
article)
It is precisely because calling the name is easy that
continuity brings rebirth
. If one can be
mindful thought after thought
to the end of life
then ten of ten are reborn, a hundred of a hundred.
May all people reflect well and, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, must
stir their minds and restrain themselves
(rouse oneself to what should be done and keep oneself from what should not be done)
without ceasing by day or night
(not ceasing in the mindfulness that continues thought after thought)
; when the preceding thought ends, rebirth follows in the very next. Forever partaking of the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and at last attaining Buddhahood, how joyful this is!

Master Shandao is a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha; his words are the words of Amitabha Buddha. How one can be reborn is, of course, settled by his word as authority! Those mindful of the Buddha must engrave this in their hearts, believing it ever more, relying on it all the more.
Concerning
the ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death bringing rebirth
, Master Shandao taught:

If I attain Buddhahood, and sentient beings in the ten directions, calling on my name, vow to be born in my land, down to as few as ten thoughts, and they are not born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
" (Commentary on the Meditation Sutra, in four fascicles)

If I become a Buddha, and sentient beings in the ten directions, wishing to be born in my land, call on my name, down to as few as ten sounds, and, relying on my vow-power, are not born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
" (The Contemplation of the Dharma Gate)
If I become a Buddha, and sentient beings in the ten directions, calling on my name, down to as few as ten sounds, are not born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The Litany of Praise for Rebirth)
The “down to ten thoughts” and “down to ten sounds” spoken of here, taken together with Master Shandao’s saying above,
“Precisely because calling the name is easy, continuity brings rebirth. If one can be
mindful thought after thought, to the end of life
, then ten of ten are reborn, a hundred of a hundred,”
clearly reveal this is an abbreviated way of saying “upward to a whole life of mindfulness thought after thought, downward to
the ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death
”, because Master Shandao had already said plainly:
“Mindful thought after thought, to the end of life.”
And
“mindful thought after thought, to the end of life”
is precisely the means by which a thought-continuing mindfulness becomes habitual and second nature,
so as to ensure the ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death
If one does not recite the Buddha at the moment of death, or recites with a scattered mind, then it is not
“mindful thought after thought, to the end of life”
Therefore,
“down to ten thoughts, and not to be born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment”
means precisely this:
ten thoughts at the moment of death; continuous, and rebirth follows.
[Ten thoughts, ten sounds] Recite the Buddha's name for ten thoughts.
[Mindfulness thought after thought becoming nature by habit] Through repeated practice without cease, one makes thought-continuing mindfulness a natural instinct.
Therefore, the condition for rebirth is:
the ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death.
[Note:
The "down to ten thoughts (ten sounds)" taught by Master Shandao is, without any doubt, the ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death, because this is
right thought at the moment of death

. In recent years, however, through the encroachment of the fundamental-vow school, right and wrong have become confused, and two other readings have appeared: first, that "down to ten thoughts (ten sounds)" means having recited the Buddha's name at least ten times in ordinary times, so that as long as one has recited ten times one is surely reborn — this is the theoretical basis for the teaching that naming brings certain rebirth; second, that "down to ten thoughts (ten sounds)" means ten thoughts (ten sounds) of scattered-minded recitation at the moment of death — this is the theoretical basis for the teaching that even scattered recitation brings certain rebirth. Both readings are wrong. For
if
one has merely
recited ten times in ordinary times yet
does not recite at the moment of death, or though reciting at the moment of death does so with a scattered mind, neither case constitutes
"mindful thought after thought, to the end of life"
Hence
"down to ten thoughts (ten sounds)"
means down to
ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death
. Therefore Master Daochuo taught clearly:
If any sentient being, even one who has committed evil through an entire life,
at the moment of death has ten continuous thoughts
calling on my name,
and is not born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The Collection on the Peaceful Land

Moreover, Master Shandao strongly emphasized wholehearted mindfulness of the Buddha (yet now some openly proclaim that Master Shandao held that naming certainly brings rebirth and that scattered recitation is sufficient). He taught:

Now there are two kinds of practice: first, the right practice; second, the mixed practice. The right practice is to practice solely in accordance with the sutras of rebirth; this is called the right practice. What is it?
Wholehearted
recitation of this Contemplation Sutra, the Amitabha Sutra, the Immeasurable Life Sutra, and so forth,
Wholehearted
focused thought, contemplation, and recollection of the two-fold splendor of that land. If bowing, then
wholehearted
bowing to that Buddha; if reciting aloud, then
wholehearted
reciting of that Buddha; if praising and making offerings, then
wholehearted
praise and offerings.
This is called the right
Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra; for the commentary,
See
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teachings
in the section "Wholehearted upholding of the Name".)
Therefore

the "down to ten thoughts (ten sounds)" taught by Master Shandao is neither "having recited ten times in ordinary times, one is certainly reborn" (the basis for naming-brings-rebirth) nor "ten scattered-mind recitations at the moment of death, one is certainly reborn" (the basis for scattered recitation), but rather
ten continuous recitations of the Buddha at the moment of death
(not interrupted by deluded thought)
, and then one is certainly reborn
Master Yongming is also a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha. Master Yongming taught:
"When walking the path
(circumambulation)
and bowing, when reciting the Buddha and making vows, with earnest and sincere devotion,
without any stray thought
, as if going to execution, as if within a prison
(a prison)

, pursued by robbers and enemies, pressed by water and fire, with a single mind seeking deliverance, vowing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly to realize the unborn, to liberate the multitude of living beings, to perpetuate the Three Jewels, and to repay the four kinds of grace — with such sincerity, one's effort will never be in vain. If words and deeds do not correspond and faith is slight, without
a thought-continuing, mindful heart
, with a mind given to frequent interruption
(the thought of recitation cut off by deluded thought)
, resting in this laxness and hoping for rebirth at death, one is only covered over by the obstacles of karma and will hardly meet a good companion
(a good teacher who could arouse right thought at the moment of death)
; as wind and fire press upon him, right thought comes to nothing. Why? Because
this present is the cause, the moment of death the fruit
; the cause must be real for the fruit not to be false. If one wishes
the ten thoughts to be accomplished at the moment of death
, one has only to prepare the means beforehand, to gather merit and virtue, and to dedicate it to that hour
(dedicate it to the moment of death)
, so that thought never falls short
(so as to accomplish mindfulness thought after thought)
, and then there is nothing to worry about."
(The Collection of Myriad Good Deeds Returning to One) This passage means:
with a mind of thought-continuing mindfulness, accomplish the ten thoughts at death. —
This is entirely in accord with Master Shandao's teaching.

[Master Yongming is also a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha] Because Master Yongming is a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, his birthday, the seventeenth day of the eleventh lunar month, was made the anniversary of Amitabha Buddha’s birth. Of Master Yongming, Master Yinguang praised him, saying:
“Master Yongming is the transformation of Amitabha Buddha. With great compassion and great mercy, he awakened and transformed sentient beings.”
The Collected Letters of Master Yinguang, in the
speech to the World Buddhist Laymen’s Forest)

[The ten thoughts accomplished at death] To accomplish the ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death. [Prepares the means beforehand] “Means” is the ferry and the bridge; to prepare the means beforehand is to make ready in advance.

As the saying goes: “To know the way up the mountain, one must ask one who has been there.” Master Tanluan and Master Daochuo are people who cultivated and realized the fruit; they are the veterans of the path of rebirth.
As for the condition for rebirth
both Master Tanluan and Master Daochuo taught:
ten thoughts at the moment of death; continuous, and rebirth follows.
(See
Master Tanluan’s Pure Land Teachings
and
Master Daochuo’s Pure Practice Teachings
This is entirely in accord with the teachings of Master Shandao and Master Yongming.
As for the
meaning
of Amitabha's fundamental vow (the eighteenth vow), Master Daochuo taught in The Collection on the Peaceful Land:
"If any sentient being, even one who has committed evil through an entire life,
at the moment of death has ten continuous thoughts
calling on my name,
and is not born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Here Master Daochuo, with regard to the
meaning of "even down to ten thoughts"
in
Amitabha's fundamental vow (the eighteenth vow)
, made a precise explanation:
at the moment of death, ten continuous thoughts calling on my name.
Therefore,
the "even down to ten thoughts"
in
Amitabha's fundamental vow (the eighteenth vow)
is the ten thoughts at the moment of death
and moreover the ten continuous thoughts
(See
The Eighteenth Vow
[Continuity] Not interrupted by deluded thought. Master Tanluan said in his Commentary on the Discourse on Rebirth:
"Mind following mind in continuity, with no other thought intruding
(no other thought mixed in)
Master Tanluan also said:
with no other mind intruding
(no other thought mixed in)
, mind after mind in succession
(one after another)
, down to ten thoughts,
this is called the ten continuous thoughts
(A Brief Treatise on the Meaning of the Peaceful Land)
Concerning
"the ten continuous thoughts and one is reborn"
, Master Tanluan taught in A Brief Treatise on the Meaning of the Peaceful Land:
"Question: In the lower class birth it is said:
'With ten continuous thoughts one is reborn.'

What is meant by the ten continuous thoughts? Answer: Suppose a person, in an open and desolate place, meets a bandit enemy, who draws his blade and, furious, comes straight at him to kill. The man runs for his life and sees a river ahead; if he can cross it, his head and neck are safe. At that time his only thought is of the means of crossing: 'When I reach the bank, shall I cross with my clothes on, or take them off? If I go in with clothes on, I fear I cannot get across; if I take them off, I fear I will have no time.' Having only this thought, with no other concern, each single thought of how to cross the river is a single thought.
Such an undistracted mind is called the ten continuous thoughts.

The practitioner is likewise: mindful of Amitabha Buddha, as that man was mindful of crossing, going through ten thoughts — whether recollecting the Buddha's name, the Buddha's marks, the Buddha's light, the Buddha's spiritual power, the Buddha's merits, the Buddha's wisdom, or the Buddha's fundamental vow.
With no other mind intruding, mind after mind in succession, down to ten thoughts — this is called the ten continuous thoughts.
(For the commentary see
Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teachings
Therefore, the condition for rebirth is:
the ten continuous thoughts at the moment of death.
That is to say:
ten thoughts at the moment of death; continuous, and rebirth follows.
Question:
Master Shandao taught:
"Continuity brings rebirth."
What does this mean?
Answer: "Continuity brings rebirth" means this:
at the moment of death, the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha continues
(not interrupted by deluded thought)
, and one is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The "continuity" here is the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha, thought after thought in succession, with no deluded thought mixed in (if deluded thought is mixed in, it is no longer continuity). One must not misunderstand the word "continuity" here as meaning the name continuing on the lips (while deluded thoughts are mixed in the mind). Of this it is said: a slip of a hair's breadth, and one errors by a thousand miles.
Question: How do we know that "continuity brings rebirth" means the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha continuing
at the moment of death
brings rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and not that, so long as one's thought of mindfulness has at some time in daily life been continuous, one is reborn at death
Answer: Master Shandao taught:
"If one can be mindful thought after thought,
to the end of life
(one who thus practices through his whole life)
, then ten of ten are reborn, a hundred of a hundred."
Note that "ten of ten are reborn, a hundred of a hundred" applies to
"one who is mindful to the end of life
(one who thus practices through his whole life)
not to one whose thought of mindfulness has merely at some time in daily life been continuous. Master Shandao continued:
"May all people reflect well and, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, must stir their minds and restrain themselves, without ceasing by day or night
(not ceasing in the mindfulness that continues thought after thought)
when the preceding thought ends, rebirth follows in the very next
. Forever partaking of the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and at last attaining Buddhahood, how joyful this is!"
(See
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teachings
in the section "Continuity brings rebirth".) So "continuity brings rebirth" means that
at the moment of death
mindfulness continuing thought after thought brings rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Stir the mind and restrain oneself] Stir the mind: to rouse oneself to do what should be done; restrain oneself: to keep oneself from doing what should not be done. These four words are the mighty weapon for overcoming difficulty and sweeping away obstacles.

Question: How do we know that the "continuity" in "continuity brings rebirth" is "the thought of mindfulness continuing," and not "the name continuing on the lips (while deluded thoughts are mixed in the mind)"?
Answer: "Continuity brings rebirth" comes from Master Shandao's Two Teachings on the Single and Mixed Practice of the Pure Land, which reads:

Question: Why not have people practice contemplation, and instead directly direct them to call exclusively on the name? Answer: Sentient beings are heavy in obstacles, the object is subtle and the mind coarse, consciousness flies and spirit scatters, so contemplation is hard to achieve. Therefore the Great Sage
(Śākyamuni Buddha)
, with compassionate pity, directly urged the exclusive calling on the name.
It is precisely because calling the name is easy
(precisely because upholding the Name is easier to accomplish than contemplative recitation)
that continuity brings rebirth
(that at the moment of death, so long as the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha continues, one is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)
. If one can be mindful thought after thought, to the end of life
(one who thus practices through his whole life)
, then ten of ten are reborn, a hundred of a hundred.
Why? Because with no external distractions,
one gains right thought
(the mind no longer grasping outward after this and that, and thus gaining right thought)

, because one accords with the Buddha's fundamental vow, because one does not contravene the teaching, because one complies with the Buddha's words. If one abandons exclusive mindfulness and practices mixed deeds, scarcely one or two in a hundred succeed, scarcely three or four in a thousand. Why? Because with distractions agitating the mind
(because the mind grasps outward after this and that)
one
loses right thought
, because one does not accord with the Buddha's fundamental vow, because one contravenes the teaching, because one does not comply with the Buddha's words, because
the connected mindfulness is not continued
because the mind does not continue in mindfulness to repay the Buddha's grace

, and though one performs practices, one is ever bound up with fame and gain; fond of clinging to distractions, one obstructs oneself and others in the right practice of rebirth. May all people reflect well and, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, must stir their minds and restrain themselves, without ceasing by day or night
(not ceasing in the mindfulness that continues thought after thought)
when the preceding thought ends, rebirth follows in the very next
. Forever partaking of the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and at last attaining Buddhahood, how joyful this is!"
(The Two Teachings on the Single and Mixed Practice of the Pure Land by Master Shandao of the Tang dynasty; for the commentary see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teachings

Notice the words in this teaching of Master Shandao: "mindful thought after thought," "gains right thought," "loses right thought," "the connected mindfulness is not continued," "the mind is not continued," "when the preceding thought ends, rebirth follows in the very next." All of these show that the "continuity" in "continuity brings rebirth" is "the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha, thought after thought in succession," and not "the name continuing on the lips (while deluded thoughts are mixed in the mind)."
Master Yinguang greatly praised this teaching, saying

“Master Shandao is the transformation of Amitabha, endowed with great spiritual powers and great wisdom. In his wide exposition of the Pure Land, he does not prize the mysterious and profound; he only teaches people to cultivate in the genuine, the real, and the ordinary.
As to the single and mixed practice he set forth, its benefits are inexhaustible.
(The Collected Letters of Master Yinguang, letter in reply to the Yongjia layman’s family)
Master Tanluan said:
with no other mind intruding
(no other thought mixed in)
, mind after mind in succession
(one after another)
, down to ten thoughts,
this is called the ten continuous thoughts
(A Brief Treatise on the Meaning of the Peaceful Land) Therefore,
continuity is with no other mind intruding
(no other thought mixed in).
Master Daochuo said:

"At the moment of death of all sentient beings, the wind-knife severs the body, the agonies of death press upon them, and great fear arises. Therefore, meeting a good teacher, they raise great vigor, and
mind after mind in continuity
through ten thoughts; this is the ever-increasing root of good, and they are reborn."
(The Collection on the Peaceful Land) Therefore,
continuity is mind continuing after mind, not the mouth continuing
As for “mindful thought after thought,” a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha,
Master Yongming taught:
“When walking the path
(circumambulation)
and bowing, when reciting the Buddha and making vows, with earnest and sincere devotion,
without any stray thought
, as if going to execution, as if within a prison
(a prison)

, pursued by robbers and enemies, pressed by water and fire, with a single mind seeking deliverance, vowing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly to realize the unborn, to liberate the multitude of living beings, to perpetuate the Three Jewels, and to repay the four kinds of grace — with such sincerity, one’s effort will never be in vain. If words and deeds do not correspond and faith is slight, without
a thought-continuing, mindful heart
, with a mind given to frequent interruption
(the thought of recitation cut off by deluded thought)
, resting in this laxness and hoping for rebirth at death, one is only covered over by the obstacles of karma and will hardly meet a good companion
(a good teacher who could arouse right thought at the moment of death)
; as wind and fire press upon him, right thought comes to nothing. Why? Because
this present is the cause, the moment of death the fruit
; the cause must be real for the fruit not to be false. If one wishes
the ten thoughts to be accomplished at the moment of death
, one has only to prepare the means beforehand, to gather merit and virtue, and to dedicate it to that hour
(dedicate it to the moment of death)
, so that thought never falls short
(so as to accomplish mindfulness thought after thought)
, and then there is nothing to worry about.”
(The Collection of Myriad Good Deeds Returning to One)

In this teaching Master Yongming plainly points out: "without a thought-continuing, mindful heart, with a mind given to frequent interruption" is exactly "words and deeds not corresponding, faith slight," is exactly laxness. Therefore,
continuity is the mind continuing thought after thought
, not the mouth continuing
The twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Chewu, taught:
“What is called holding to the name is the meaning of
clasping it firmly to the breast
(holding it fast in mind)
, that is, holding it firmly in the mind never forgetting it for an instant. The slightest
break in a single thought
and it is no longer holding. The slightest
mixture of a single thought
and it is no longer holding.
Mind thought after thought in continuity, without mixture or break
, is true vigor. With unceasing vigor, one gradually enters samadhi of one-pointed mind and completes the pure karma.”

(The Collected Works of Master Chewu) That is to say: the thought of mindfulness of the Buddha not cut off by deluded thought, not mixed with deluded thought, is called mindfulness thought after thought in continuity.
Therefore, mindfulness thought after thought is free of the mixture of deluded thought.
[Clasping it firmly to the breast (
yīng

)] Clasping: to hold fast without letting go, extended to mean earnest sincerity; to the breast: to hold it in mind. "Clasping it firmly to the breast" describes remembering it earnestly and never forgetting.
As for what is meant by the ten recitations in unbroken succession,
Master Tanluan explained it in his Brief Discourse on the Peace and Bliss of the Pure Land (see the article
Master Tanluan's Teachings on the Pure Land

For example, a man in an open wilderness meets a bandit foe who draws his blade, races forward, and means to kill him. The man runs for his life and sees a river ahead; if he can cross it, his life is saved. At that moment his one thought is only of how to cross: 'When I reach the bank, shall I cross in my clothes, or strip them off? If I keep my clothes, I fear I may not get across; if I take them off, I fear there will be no time.' Holding only this thought, with no other concern, his single thought is just this: how to get across the river.
To be undivided like this is what is called the ten recitations in unbroken succession.

Answer: For example, a man in the wilderness meets a foe and thief who draws a blade and charges at him to kill him. The man runs for his life and sees a great river; if he can cross it, his life will be saved. At that time his only thought is how best to cross: 'When I reach the bank, shall I swim in my clothes, or take them off? If I keep my clothes on, I fear I will not get across; if I take them off, I fear there is no time.' At that moment he has only the thought of crossing and nothing else, just this single thought: how to cross the river? That alone is the thought. To be undivided by any other thought in this way is called the ten recitations in unbroken succession.
The practitioner is likewise: he recites Amitabha Buddha as that man thought only of crossing, pressing straight
(the same as jing, meaning 'straight on')
on to the ten recitations: whether he recollects the Buddha's name, his auspicious marks, his light, his spiritual powers, his virtues and merit, his wisdom, or his primal vows.
With no other thought mixed in, thought follows thought up to the tenth, and this is called the ten recitations in unbroken succession.

The practitioner is the same: single-mindedly he recites Amitabha Buddha, as that man single-mindedly thought only of crossing the river, and so he goes straight on for ten recitations, whether he recollects the Buddha's name, his auspicious marks, his light, his spiritual powers, his virtues, his wisdom, or his primal vow. With no other thought mixed in, thought follows thought up to the tenth recitation, and this is called the ten recitations in unbroken succession.
Xiangci: one following another in succession.
Question: What is the relationship between the ten recitations in unbroken succession at death and single-minded, undistracted concentration?
Answer: Single-minded, undistracted concentration refers to ordinary daily practice, and it is the most reliable guarantee of the ten recitations in unbroken succession at death.

Therefore past teachers were very particular about holding to a single thought, and they cultivated in accord with the single-minded, undistracted concentration described in the sutra spoken by the Buddha on Amitabha. Since the minimum requirement for rebirth is:
the ten recitations in unbroken succession at death
(see
The Primal Vows of Amitabha
article
So Master Tanluan, Master Daochuo, and Master Shandao, moved by great compassion, earnestly taught those who recite the Buddha's name to take the ten recitations in unbroken succession and make it
second nature through long practice
, so as to ensure the ten recitations in unbroken succession at death and thus be reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. (See
Master Tanluan's Teachings on the Pure Land
Master Daochuo's Teachings on Pure Practice
and
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching

) Moreover, when the practice of the continuous ten recitations deepens, one achieves a hundred recitations in succession, and then a thousand in succession. And as it becomes continuous at all times, one reaches the state of single-minded, undistracted concentration.
Xijichengxing: through repeated practice to make the continuous ten recitations a part of one's very nature. (See
Ten Recitations at Death, Continuous and Thus Reborn
article.)
Question:
What is the relationship between making the continuous ten recitations second nature, and faith and vows?
Answer: to
make the continuous ten recitations second nature is a long process of unremitting practice. Master Shandao said:
“Recitation following recitation without break, and so to the end of one's life
(to practise thus for one's whole life)
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must
rouse the mind and restrain oneself
; day and night never give up
(never stop the recitation following recitation, day or night)
(The Doctrine of the Two Cultivations, the Whole and the Mixed.)

In this process one must remove many obstacles and distractions, overcome many difficulties and temptations, and, facing setbacks and hard passes, never give up. One meets challenges with zeal and perseverance, and can endure hardship. Without faith leading the way and

vows as the driving force, one cannot keep going. At the same time, whether one can persist in this way is itself the concrete expression of faith and vows, and a real testing of them, showing where one's weak spots lie and how to deepen faith and vows. And as the practice of making the continuous ten recitations second nature grows ever deeper, the strength of faith and vows also grows deeper and more genuine. Thus faith, vows, and practice are inseparable and mutually reinforcing. As the Master Xiu Wu, who knew the hour of his coming, spoke from experience before he left:
“To be able to speak yet not to practise
(to speak of faith and vow only with the mouth, without the actual deed that realizes faith and fulfils the vow)
, that is not true wisdom.”
(See
Examples of Rebirth
article.) And Master Yinguang said
“One should rouse
genuine

vows: to be free from the suffering of the Saha world and to attain the bliss of Ultimate Bliss. The urgency of these vows should be like one fallen into a latrine yearning for escape, or a prisoner in chains longing for home.”
(The Collected Letters of Master Yinguang, letter to the layman Chen Xizhou.)

When one meets setbacks and hard times, whether one breaks through by deliberate practice or chooses to give up, that is the real test of faith and vows, and the dividing line between success and failure.
The Buddha said:
“Though one labours diligently for a single lifetime, in an instant one is reborn in the land of Immeasurable Life, with joy beyond measure.”
(The Sutra of Immeasurable Life spoken by the Buddha.)
Master Shandao said:
“Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, and day and night never give up.
When the previous thought ends this life, the next thought is already reborn.
Forever enjoying the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood, how delightful!”
(The Doctrine of the Two Cultivations, the Whole and the Mixed.)
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, in his verse of reminder to the multitude, said:
“This day is already past, and life diminishes with it; like a fish in dying water, what
(this)
joy is there? O assembly: be diligent and vigorous, as if saving your head from a blaze! Think only of impermanence
(think only of the coming of death)
, and be by no means heedless
(in no way give yourself over to ease and pleasure)
Shaoshui yu: a fish in a pond whose water is drying up day by day.
Dang qin jingjin, ru jiu tou ran:
A great fire is burning on one's head and death is rushing close; one who recites the Buddha's name should
be diligent and untiring,
quickly
, and

hasten to put out this fire of death, and, before falling into the darkness and dying, achieve the ten recitations made second nature by continuous practice. Wuchang (impermanence): nothing abides, all things in the world arise and cease, flowing on without a moment's rest; it also refers to death and the spirit that summons the soul. Shen wu fangyi: by no means be heedless, in no way give oneself over to ease and pleasure and waste spirit and time.
Maxim:

In the eyes of the successful, failure is not merely a temporary setback but an opportunity as well: it shows that some lack or deficiency exists in you. Find it, mend the gap, and you have gained experience, ability, and wisdom, taking a great step toward success. The most important reason the failed fail is that they lack enthusiasm and perseverance; at the first taste of setback they sound the retreat. There is only one true failure in the world, and that is losing enthusiasm and perseverance and giving up easily.
For one who recites the Buddha's name, enthusiasm and perseverance come from deep faith and earnest vows, and they are also the concrete expression of that deep faith and earnest vows.

Question: Since faith, vows, and practice are inseparable, why does Master Ouyi say in his Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sutra that 'if there is no faith or vow, though one uphold the Name until the wind cannot penetrate it and the rain cannot wet it, like a wall of silver and iron, there is still no reason to attain rebirth'?

Answer: Those who 'uphold the Name without faith or vow until the wind cannot penetrate and the rain cannot wet, like a wall of silver and iron' are those Chan practitioners who treat the Buddha-name as a huatou to meditate upon. They were never practising the Pure Land in the first place; their faith is the faith of Chan, to see one's own nature and become a Buddha, and their vow is likewise to attain that goal of 'seeing one's own nature and attaining Buddhahood.' So their recitation of the Buddha's name is not Pure Land practice but Chan meditation. I ask you: if a Pure Land practitioner could recite until the wind cannot penetrate and the rain cannot wet, like a wall of silver and iron, could you still say he lacks faith and vow? And without faith and vow as the guide, the motive force, the encouragement, the spur, and the supervision, could recitation ever reach that state?

Master Ouyi made this remark to warn those Chan practitioners that they should cultivate both Chan and Pure Land. For 'to uphold the Name until the wind cannot penetrate and the rain cannot wet, like a wall of silver and iron' is already, in Pure Land practice, entirely the state of single-minded, undistracted concentration; if faith and vow are complete, one will surely be reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, ending birth-and-death and escaping the wheel of transmigration. But in Chan meditation, to end birth-and-death and escape the wheel, one must pass through all thoughts returning to one, the one returning to nothing, and seeing one's own nature; then one does the work of maintaining, until the afflictions of false views and false thinking are completely cut off, and only then can one end birth-and-death and escape the wheel. 'To uphold the Name until the wind cannot penetrate and the rain cannot wet, like a wall of silver and iron' is only the first stage of Chan practice, the gathering of a thousand thoughts into one, and it is still far from ending birth-and-death and escaping transmigration. So Master Yongming, who was a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, and many other great masters of the patriarchs, again and again urged Chan practitioners to cultivate both Chan and Pure Land.
On cultivating both Chan and Pure Land, Master Ouyi said:
“A Chan practitioner who wishes to be born in the West need not change to reciting the Buddha's name; if he has faith and vow, then his Chan meditation itself is the practice of the Pure Land.”
(Master Ouyi's Pure Land Collection
Chats in the Brahma Chamber.)
Question: Master Ouyi said,
“Whether one attains rebirth depends wholly on the presence or absence of faith and vow; the grade of one's status depends wholly on the depth or shallowness of one's recitation of the name.”
Therefore, as long as one has faith and vow, one attains rebirth.
Answer: This is a mistaken understanding of Master Ouyi's teaching. Why it is mistaken, see
Whether One Attains Rebirth
article.
Question: Master Shandao said,

“With single-minded faith and joy, seeking and vowing to be reborn: from the full span of a lifetime down to ten recitations, riding the power of the Buddha's vows, all without exception attain rebirth.”
Therefore, as long as one recites the Buddha's name in a distracted frame of mind even ten times in daily life, one will surely be reborn. Is that so?

Answer: 'from the full span of a lifetime' refers to 'one who recites thought after thought without break and so to the end of life'; the 'ten recitations' in 'down to ten recitations' refers to 'the ten recitations in succession at death.' 'Down to ten recitations' in no way means that one who recites the name ten times in a distracted state during ordinary life will surely attain rebirth. Master Shandao said:
If one can recite thought after thought without break
and to the end of one's life
(one who practises thus for his whole life)
, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. ...... I wish all people to reflect well:
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, and day and night never give up
(never stop the recitation following recitation, day or night)
; when the previous thought ends this life, the next thought is already reborn. Forever enjoying the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood, how delightful!”
(See
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
, in the section on 'continuous and thus reborn.') Here Master Shandao clearly teaches:

one should recite thought after thought without break, and so to the end of life; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, and day and night never give up.
Yet the Primal Vow school has brazenly taken 'down to ten recitations,'
and distorted it into
the claim that even one who recites the name ten times in a distracted state during daily life will surely be reborn. For the refutation of these fallacies, see
Is Reciting the Name Enough for Rebirth?
article.
As for how one can be reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, Master Shandao set it forth with perfect clarity:
“Precisely because reciting the name is easy,
being continuous, one is at once reborn

. If one can recite thought after thought without break and so to the end of life, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. ...... I wish all people to reflect well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself, and day and night never give up. When the previous thought ends this life, the next thought is already reborn. Forever enjoying the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood, how delightful!”
(See
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching

Zheng wei chengming yi gu: precisely because the practice of holding the Buddha's name is easier to succeed at than visualising meditation. Xiangxu ji sheng: at the moment of death, as long as one's thought of recitation continues without break (not cut off by false thoughts), one is at once reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. Biming wei qi zhe: one who practises thus for his whole life. Lixin keji: lixin, to spur one's mind to do what should be done; keji, to restrain oneself from doing what should not be done. These four characters 'lixin keji' are a mighty weapon for overcoming difficulties and removing obstacles. Here 'li' is the same as 'li', the character meaning 'to rouse.' For example: 'With firm armour and whetted weapons, prepare against trouble.' (Han Feizi,
The Five Vermin.) 'Keji': to restrain oneself. Zhouye mo fei: do not stop the recitation following recitation, day or night.

Master Shandao is a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, and we must understand his teachings in their full and exact sense and practise them obediently. If one takes passages out of context, distorts them at will, and acts contrary to them, the consequence is:
not only failing to be reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, but also falling into the fate of slandering the Buddha and destroying the Dharma.

Fan qi dao er xing zhi (to act contrary to the way): Master Shandao, a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, taught 'being continuous, one is at once reborn.' The Primal Vow school, however, loudly proclaims 'reciting the name surely attains rebirth' and 'even distracted recitation surely attains rebirth.'
Question: Master Daochuo said in the Collection on Peace and Bliss:

“If any sentient being, even one who has committed evil throughout his life, at the moment of death recites my name in ten thoughts in unbroken succession, and is not reborn, then may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”

Since 'even one who has committed evil throughout his life' will surely be reborn as long as at death there are 'ten thoughts in unbroken succession,' is there then no need to abandon evil and practise good?

Answer: 'Even one who has committed evil throughout his life, so long as at death the ten thoughts continue in unbroken succession, will surely be reborn' shows that right mindfulness at death (the ten thoughts in unbroken succession) is of utmost importance. That is to say: the ten thoughts in unbroken succession at death are the sole requirement for rebirth; as long as the ten thoughts are unbroken at death, one can move Amitabha Buddha to come and welcome one. But to meet this requirement, in daily life one must make the ten thoughts in unbroken succession second nature, and abandoning evil and practising good are very important auxiliary conditions. So Master Shandao taught:
“I wish all people to reflect well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
one must rouse the mind and restrain oneself

, and day and night never give up. When the previous thought ends this life, the next thought is already reborn. Forever enjoying the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, and even attaining Buddhahood, how delightful!”
The words in his teaching
'rouse the mind and restrain oneself'

mean to spur oneself on and to restrain oneself. A person who gives free rein to evil is incapable of 'rousing the mind and restraining himself,' and this is also out of accord with single-minded recitation free of stray thoughts.
On this point, the Contemplator of Compassion Master Ciyun taught:

“When the mind is thus bound to the Buddha, it naturally always wards off all evil thoughts by itself. Even if one were about to do evil, because of recollecting the Buddha the evil cannot come to be. Even if one follows evil and does an evil deed, the mind is still naturally softened, as a body that bears perfume naturally keeps away from smell.”
The Two Gates of Resolving Doubts and Cultivating Faith and Vows for Rebirth in the Pure Land

So the person who does not rouse the mind and restrain himself has no guarantee of the ten thoughts in unbroken succession at death. Though there are extremely rare exceptions, 'even one who has committed evil throughout his life' yet manages 'at the moment of death, ten thoughts in unbroken succession,' one must never imitate them, for hardly one arises among ten thousand reborn persons. This principle has been taught and discussed in countless ways by the great masters and patriarchs from ancient times.
For example,
Master Ouyi
said
The sutras say that one who has committed the ten evils and the five deadly offences still attains rebirth,
which must be because he once planted the seed of bodhi in the past.
Without the seed of bodhi, how could he meet a good friend? And even if he met a good friend to rouse him, how could he instantly give rise to faith and vow and recite the great name?”
(The Collected Treatises of Lingfeng,
General Discourse at Tianma Monastery in Shepu.)
Master Ouyi also said:
As for the ten thoughts at death,
one must have deeply planted wholesome roots.

Now when adverse or favourable conditions arise, one no longer has right mindfulness, how much less at death? Moreover, when the suffering of death appears, one only relies on a good friend to remind and guide; now, in broad daylight, one still cannot faithfully accept and practise the true words of a wise teacher and good friend!”
(The Collected Treatises of Lingfeng,
Preface to the Samadhi Repentance for the Pure Land and the Society for Releasing Life.)

(Translation: To achieve the ten thoughts at death one must have deeply planted wholesome roots. Now if, when adverse or favourable conditions arise, one no longer has right mindfulness, how much less can one maintain right mindfulness at death? Moreover, in broad daylight, in full clarity, one still cannot faithfully accept and practise a wise teacher's and good friend's true admonitions, how could one, when the suffering of death appears, rely only on the prompting and teaching of a good friend to be able to faithfully accept and practise?)
Question: I read Master Daozheng's article 'Clarifying the Conditions for Rebirth,' which says:
“Recently someone, very anxious and heavy of heart, told this humble one
(Master Daozheng's self-designation)

that the leader of one of Taiwan's major deathbed-assistance groups had a very bad death and was not reborn in the West. In addition, another person said, very dejected, that a certain master who had bowed to the Buddha two million five hundred thousand times also had a bad death, and perhaps was not reborn in the West either.”
How could this be?
Answer: These two did not get clear on the conditions for rebirth, and in daily life they did not cultivate in accord with those conditions,
so at death they did not achieve the continuity that means rebirth, and drifted away following their karma.

Of these two, one was the leader of one of Taiwan's major deathbed-assistance groups and the other was a monastic who had bowed to the Buddha two million five hundred thousand times. One cannot say they were not diligent,
but unfortunately they did not apply their effort to the crucial point.
If they had consistently, in daily life, applied themselves to
'the ten thoughts continuing in unbroken succession, made second nature,'
why would the outcome have been like this? This is a truly painful lesson, enough to make one sigh and wring one's hands without end.
The overturned cart ahead is a warning to the cart behind.
You who recite the Buddha's name should think on this, think on it again, and think on it once more!
Do not let this tragedy repeat itself upon yourselves.
Question: There is a saying: 'Though one recites the Buddha's name in a distracted state, as long as faith and vow are complete, one will surely be reborn.' Is this saying correct?
Answer: The claim that 'if one has true faith and earnest vows, even distracted recitation of the name can attain rebirth'
is fundamentally fallacious!
It is what tears faith and vow apart from practice.
Faith, vow, and practice are linked ring to ring in an indivisible whole. The relationship among them is:
faith initiates the vow, and the vow guides the practice; practice fulfils the vow, and practice certifies the faith.
Of the many makers of fallacies,
the common mark
is that they tear faith and vow apart from practice. Some even proclaim: as long as there is faith and vow, one attains rebirth! Faith itself is rebirth!
The Buddha and the patriarchs have again and again taught single-minded recitation of the Buddha's name, and again and again urged that one practise according to the teaching (see
Commentary on the Sutra Praising the Pure Land and Its Buddha's Reception
). Therefore, one of complete faith and vow is certain to practise according to the teaching and recite single-mindedly (see
Single-Minded Recitation, Not Distracted Recitation
). The one who recites in a distracted state, because he dreads hardship and suffering, acts contrary to the Buddha's and the patriarchs' teaching, and
this is precisely the concrete sign of unreal faith and unearnest vows
(see the teaching of Master Yongming, manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, below). Therefore,
the one who recites in a distracted state
is, as Master Yongming said,
'one whose power of faith is slight.'
Therefore, the distracted reciter's faith and vows are surely not genuine.
The case of 'distracted recitation yet true faith and earnest vows' simply does not exist;
it is a false proposition
, just as a brave warrior who cowers at the front ranks does not exist.

Since this case does not exist, how can there be any talk of rebirth or not? Therefore 'though one recites the name in a distracted state, as long as faith and vow are complete, one will surely be reborn' is a fallacy.
Weimingti (false proposition): an untrue proposition. Mingti (proposition): a declarative sentence expressing a judgement.
Master Yongming
in
the Collected All-Good Return of Myriad Good Deeds
taught:
“If one's words and deeds do not match,
and the power of faith is slight,
so that there is no mind of thought following thought without break, but a mind that breaks off again and again
(that is, distracted recitation)
then, relying on one's indolence
and hoping for rebirth at death, one is likely to be blocked by the hindrance of karma; it is hard to meet a good friend, as the elements of wind and fire press close,
right mindfulness is not achieved.
In this teaching Master Yongming clearly points out: why does one recite in a distracted state (
'a mind with no thought following thought without break, but a mind that breaks off again and again'
)? It is because
'words and deeds do not match, and the power of faith is slight.'
Therefore the one whose words match his deeds, with genuine faith and earnest vows, is certain to recite single-mindedly.
And distracted recitation precisely shows that this person is
'one whose words and deeds do not match, whose power of faith is slight.'
. Moreover Master Yongming particularly points out: distracted recitation is an act of indolence, and going on in this indolence (
'relying on one's indolence'
), at the time of death
'as the elements of wind and fire press close, right mindfulness is not achieved,'
and so one does not attain rebirth.

Yanxing bu cheng (words and deeds not matching): words and deeds are out of accord, one says with the mouth that he has true faith and earnest vows, yet his actual conduct is indolent (neither true nor earnest):
'a mind with no thought following thought without break, but a mind that breaks off again and again.'

Question: Why is it that only right mindfulness at death (the ten thoughts in unbroken succession at death) enables rebirth? Amitabha Buddha's five kalpas of contemplation, his immeasurable kalpas of practice, his whole great vow, all are meant to save every sentient being. With such a great compassionate heart, would he not exercise his majestic spiritual power and vow at the moment of our death to come and welcome us?
Answer:

At the death of every sentient being, Amitabha Buddha is there to welcome him. It is only that sentient beings without right mindfulness at death cannot see it, and so they follow their own deluded thoughts, and according to their karma are cast into another birth.
Therefore one must have right mindfulness at death to see Amitabha Buddha come and welcome him, and so follow the Buddha to be reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss.
On this principle, Master Zhongfeng, praised as an ancient Buddha of the Jiangnan region, taught in the Three Seasons of Recollection:
“Although it is said that Amitabha takes in sentient beings and brings them to rebirth, one must believe that it is
only as the mind itself manifests,
the mutual response between the mind's call and the Buddha's answer,
and in the end
(after all)
is not obtained from without.

Weishi suixin zixian (only as the mind itself manifests): Amitabha Buddha comes to welcome (take in) sentient beings, and it is only because this manifests from the mind itself, the mutual response between the mind's call and the Buddha's answer, not attained from without. Therefore only one with right mindfulness at death can see the Buddha come, while the others around him cannot see it. For the dying sentient beings without right mindfulness at death, because their own minds are turbid and confused, there is no stirring of right mindfulness (the ten thoughts in unbroken succession), and so naturally the Buddha's welcoming does not respond within the mind and they cannot see the Buddha come. It is not that Amitabha Buddha did not come to welcome them.
Therefore, whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has right mindfulness at death
(the ten thoughts in unbroken succession at death)
This is why
both Master Shandao, a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, and Master Yongming, a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, earnestly taught:
one must accomplish the ten thoughts in unbroken succession at death
(see
The Eighteenth Vow
. This is the teaching of Amitabha Buddha himself!
Ganying dao jiao (mutual response between the mind's call and the Buddha's answer): the call of sentient beings and the response of Amitabha Buddha interpenetrate each other.

On the principle of the mind's call and the Buddha's response at death, Master Yinguang, who is a manifestation of the Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta, said in the Preface to the Guide to Pure Karma for Beginners:

“The mind of sentient beings is like water, and Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings are complete in faith and vow and with utmost sincerity move the Buddha, the Buddha responds to them, just as when the water is clear the moon appears. If the mind is not pure, is not sincere, is in accord with greed, anger, and delusion, and runs contrary to the Buddha, it is like murky, restless water: the moon does not fail to shine upon it, yet it cannot reflect the moon's image distinctly.”

Translation: The mind of sentient beings is like water, and Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings are complete in faith and vow and with utmost sincerity move the Buddha, the Buddha responds, just as when the water is clear and still the moon appears (a metaphor for the pure mind of right mindfulness stirring the response of Amitabha Buddha's welcome). If the mind is not pure, is not sincere, is in accord with greed, anger, and delusion, and runs contrary to the Buddha, it is like murky, restless water: the Buddha-moon does not fail to shine upon it (a metaphor that Amitabha Buddha is always welcoming every dying sentient being), yet it cannot reflect the moon's image distinctly (a metaphor that a restless, murky mind cannot stir the response of Amitabha Buddha's welcome,
but instead follows its own deluded thoughts and, according to its karma, is cast into another birth

“Only when the water is clear and still does it appear; when the water is muddy and moving, it is hidden. The moon, to be sure, makes no choosing or rejecting. That it does not appear is only because the water is muddy and turbulent and has no way to receive its reflection.”

Translation: Only when the water is clear and still does the moon’s reflection appear; when the water is muddy and moving, the reflection does not appear. The moon, to be sure, shines upon all without choosing or rejecting; that it does not appear is because the water is muddy and turbulent and cannot present the reflection. (Analogy: Only those beings who maintain right mindfulness at the moment of death can see Amitabha Buddha’s coming to receive them, while beings without right mindfulness at death cannot see him. Amitabha Buddha, to be sure, receives every dying being without choosing or rejecting; that those without right mindfulness at death cannot see his reception is because their
own mind is muddy and
scattered,
thereupon they
follow their own delusions and, in accord with their karma, go on to be reborn

Therefore, for one who recites the Buddha’s name, single-minded right mindfulness at the moment of death is utterly important. Those who recite a thousand times, ten thousand times, even from morning till night and all the year round,
do so only to ripen this one thought of Buddha-recitation
so as to ensure that at the moment of death this thought continues unbroken and brings forth the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha’s reception
. Therefore Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, and Master Yongming, also the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, both earnestly instructed:
one must bring about the continuity of ten recitations at the moment of death
This is sacred speech!
If one will not listen to the words of Amitabha Buddha, whose words will one listen to?
do so only to ripen this one thought of Buddha-recitation
The twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Chewu, taught:

“Therefore we, for this one word ‘Amitabha,’ recite a thousand times, ten thousand times, from morning till night and all the year round, only to ripen this single thought. If once this thought becomes fully ripe, then at the moment of death there is only this one thought, with no other thought.”
